architectural_implications.after: Explicit external state store with defined lifecycle, sharing semantics, and encapsulation boundaries; the model context becomes a derived, disposable view over that state.
architectural_implications.before: Context window treated as the agent's memory; conversation history is the state store.
architectural_implications.consequence: Enables multi-agent shared state and reproducible replay, but forces engineers to design serialization, invalidation, and context-assembly logic — the new core of agent runtime work.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent state currently lives implicitly in the KV cache, which is bounded and not shareable across agents.

architectural_implications.after: Pipeline decomposed into stages, each with a machine-checkable post-condition, with code-level decision logic interleaved between model calls.
architectural_implications.before: One agent call chain executed end-to-end, with a human reviewing the final output.
architectural_implications.consequence: Reliability becomes a property of the harness rather than the model; failures localize to a stage, and rollback/repair is possible without re-running the whole chain.
architectural_implications.observation: End-to-end autonomy is unreliable, but individually verifiable stages are not.

architectural_implications.after: Treat the model as one unreliable component inside a software system that supplies the verification, state, and control flow the model lacks.
architectural_implications.before: Assume the best benchmark model is the best automation engine; invest in prompting to close the gap.
architectural_implications.consequence: Architecture investment shifts from prompt engineering to decomposition, encapsulation, and state management — and model selection becomes a component-selection decision, not a capability-selection decision.
architectural_implications.observation: RLHF-optimized models are mismatched to autonomous execution.

article_ideas.angle: Architectural critique that reframes a prompting/scaffolding problem as a training-objective problem, then draws the concrete consequence: harness design must assume the mismatch rather than attempt to erase it.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and platform architects building agents for production automation
article_ideas.thesis: Agent reliability is bounded by the post-training objective, not by scaffolding sophistication; harness engineering supplies the verification the training objective omitted, but it does not supply the missing automation policy, and conflating the two is why teams keep shipping demos that never reach unattended production.
article_ideas.title: You Get What You Optimize For: Why Your Agent Framework Cannot Fix an Assistance-Tuned Model

article_ideas.angle: Engineering-practice argument with a concrete design rule, positioned against the vibe-coding default of one long agent chain with a human reviewing the final output.
article_ideas.audience: Practitioners designing multi-stage LLM pipelines and agent runtimes
article_ideas.based_on: Task decomposition should be driven by verifiability
article_ideas.thesis: Chained probabilistic components compound error multiplicatively, so the only decomposition that produces reliability is one where every stage boundary is a machine-checkable post-condition; logical or semantic decomposition feels natural and systematically fails at the 100%-correctness bar.
article_ideas.title: Design for the Test, Not the Diagram: Verifiability as the Decomposition Rule for Agent Workflows

article_ideas.angle: Architecture piece that locates the correct engineering boundary — persistence, invalidation, and sharing belong in the runtime layer — and spells out the serialization and context-assembly work this newly creates.
article_ideas.audience: Backend and systems engineers building multi-agent runtimes
article_ideas.based_on: The KV cache is the binding architectural constraint on agents
article_ideas.thesis: Treating the context window as agent memory produces non-reproducible, non-shareable, silently degrading systems; state must become an explicit external artifact with a lifecycle, and the context window a disposable derived view over it.
article_ideas.title: The KV Cache Is Not Your State Store

article_ideas.angle: Argument piece that reframes engineering leverage away from scale and toward task and data design, using the pre-training-versus-alignment task distinction as the worked example.
article_ideas.audience: Applied ML leads and technical decision-makers without frontier training budgets
article_ideas.based_on: The 'bitterer lesson': task selection and data dominate compute and algorithm choice
article_ideas.thesis: When a capability is missing, the default hypothesis is 'we need more compute,' but the higher-leverage hypothesis is 'we are asking for the wrong task'; task formulation and data curation are actionable for teams that cannot train models at all.
article_ideas.title: Bitterer Than the Bitter Lesson: Task Selection as the Cheapest Lever You Are Not Pulling

connections.relationship: The training objective is the causal explanation offered for why models excel at assisted reasoning yet fail at unattended execution.
A bounded, non-shareable memory primitive is the reason state management must be pushed into the software layer.
Per-stage machine-checkable outputs are the mechanism that converts unreliable components into a system meeting a 100% reliability requirement.
A single missing primitive (a new color of LED / a new class of AI-native abstraction) can unlock an entire adjacent design space rather than incrementally improving the existing one.
The choice of training task, not compute, is framed as what determines which capability emerges — making alignment task choice an architectural decision.

evidence_quotes.text: 100% of LLMs today are optimized for assistance via RLHF.
You get what you optimize for.

core_insights.generalization: Whenever a system is optimized against a proxy objective (human preference, helpfulness ratings), downstream autonomous use inherits the proxy's blind spots; the harness must supply the verification the training objective omitted.
core_insights.insight: The post-training objective, not raw model capability, determines whether a model is deployable in an autonomous loop. RLHF trains for *assistance* (helpful, human-in-the-loop, conversational), which produces models that score well on reasoning benchmarks but are structurally unsuited to unverified *automation*.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes agent reliability as a training-objective problem rather than a prompting or scaffolding problem: no amount of harness engineering fully converts an assistance-tuned policy into a reliable automation policy, so harness design must assume and compensate for that mismatch.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents are constrained by the KV cache and lack shared state and memory management.

core_insights.generalization: In any system whose long-term memory is a bounded, non-shareable cache, correctness requires an external state authority; treating the cache as the state store produces silent, non-reproducible failures at scale.
core_insights.insight: The KV cache is the binding architectural constraint on agents: it is the only memory a model actually has, and it provides neither shared state nor memory management. Agent state therefore has to be an explicit, externally managed artifact rather than something left implicit in context.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It locates the correct architectural boundary: state management, memory lifecycle, and inter-agent sharing belong in the runtime/software layer, not inside the model context. This directly determines where you build persistence, invalidation, and encapsulation.

evidence_quotes.text: Getting 95% accuracy on general tasks is useless if reliability is needed 100% of the time.

core_insights.generalization: For long-horizon or chained tasks, per-step accuracy compounds multiplicatively; the optimal architecture minimizes chain depth and maximizes per-step verifiability rather than maximizing per-step generality.
core_insights.insight: Reliability requirements are binary, not average-case: ~95% general-task accuracy is worthless when the workflow demands 100% correctness. This inverts the usual scaling instinct — narrow, hyper-verifiable workflows beat broad, general capability in production automation.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It justifies deliberately constraining agent scope and inserting verification gates, and it explains why benchmark gains do not translate into automation gains for real users.

evidence_quotes.text: Break tasks down into verifiable stages.

core_insights.generalization: Any composition of probabilistic components should be partitioned at boundaries where outputs are machine-checkable; this is the same principle as designing for testability in classical software.
core_insights.insight: Task decomposition should be driven by verifiability, not by logical or semantic decomposition: break work into stages whose outputs can be checked, so that each stage boundary is a place where a deterministic or programmatic check can halt or correct the pipeline.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete design rule for agent workflows — the decomposition boundary is chosen for its testability, which is what makes the compound system reliable despite unreliable components.

evidence_quotes.text: Data always matters more than compute.
Doing the right task is the ultimate driver of performance breakthroughs.

core_insights.generalization: When a capability is missing, the first hypothesis should be 'we are training/asking for the wrong task', not 'we need more compute'.
core_insights.insight: The 'bitterer lesson': task selection and data dominate compute and algorithm choice. The pre-training task (next-token prediction) versus the alignment task (RLHF) is presented as the decisive variable in what capability emerges.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It shifts engineering leverage away from scale and toward task formulation — i.e., what you ask the model to do and what data you show it — which is an actionable, low-cost lever for teams that cannot train models.

evidence_quotes.text: What would semantic dependent typing look like in production codebases?

core_insights.generalization: Natural-language specifications should be compiled into enforceable interface constraints; anything left in prose is an unverified assumption.
core_insights.insight: The proposed frontier primitive is semantic dependent typing: types whose validity depends on semantic content and on prior values, applied to LLM inputs/outputs so that a program can statically constrain what a model is allowed to emit at each interface.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If realized, it moves LLM I/O contracts from natural-language prompt instructions (soft, unenforced) to checked interfaces (hard, enforceable), which changes where safety and correctness guarantees live in an agent codebase.

project_ideas.based_on: Ablate: same model, same task, varying only decomposition granularity and verification density
project_ideas.hypothesis: At fixed model and fixed task, increasing decomposition granularity and verification density raises end-to-end task success on a chained workflow, but with diminishing returns that plateau well below 100% — quantifying exactly how much harness design can substitute for task-aligned training.
project_ideas.measurement: End-to-end success rate per configuration, per-stage failure localization rate, tokens per successful task, and the residual failure rate at maximum verification density (the plateau that harness design cannot cross).
project_ideas.name: Verification-Density Ablation Harness
project_ideas.poc: Take one multi-step operational workflow. Run the same model under four configurations: single end-to-end call chain; stage decomposition with no checks; stage decomposition with machine-checkable post-conditions and code-level gating; and stage decomposition plus an external state store. Same model, same task, only harness varied.

project_ideas.based_on: Prototype external state stores with explicit read/write APIs and context-assembly policies
project_ideas.hypothesis: An explicit external state store with a defined lifecycle and a context-assembly policy that materializes only what a stage needs will match or beat a long-context baseline on multi-turn agent task success while substantially reducing tokens consumed — and will additionally enable replay and cross-agent state sharing that the baseline cannot express at all.
project_ideas.measurement: Task success rate, prompt tokens per turn and per task, degradation curve as task length approaches context limits, and replayability (whether a run can be deterministically reconstructed from stored state).
project_ideas.name: Context-Assembly Gateway
project_ideas.poc: Wrap a multi-turn agent workload behind a state service exposing explicit read/write APIs plus an encapsulation boundary per agent role. Context is derived per stage from the store rather than accumulated. Run identical task suites against the same model with a long-context accumulated-window baseline.

project_ideas.based_on: Build a constrained-decoding / schema layer whose validity predicates depend on runtime values
project_ideas.hypothesis: A meaningful fraction of invalid LLM outputs can be rejected statically at the interface — via validity predicates that depend on semantic content and on prior stage values — before any post-hoc evaluation runs, shrinking the error surface that a downstream verifier must handle.
project_ideas.measurement: Share of invalid outputs rejected pre-execution versus only caught post-hoc, false-rejection rate on valid outputs, and end-to-end task success with the checker versus schema-only validation.
project_ideas.name: Value-Dependent Interface Checker
project_ideas.poc: Implement a constrained-decoding plus schema layer whose type predicates reference runtime values from earlier pipeline stages (e.g., an emitted amount must reconcile against a previously emitted subtotal). Apply it to one narrow, hyper-verifiable workflow and count rejections by category.

project_ideas.based_on: Design paired benchmarks where the same underlying operation is presented as a benchmark-style reasoning problem
project_ideas.hypothesis: The same underlying operation presented as a benchmark-style reasoning problem and as an operational automation step yields a significant accuracy gap, which means benchmark scores are a contaminated proxy for production automation readiness.
project_ideas.measurement: Per-pair accuracy delta between framings, correlation between benchmark-framed score and operational-framed score, and whether models ranked by benchmark score retain that ranking under operational framing.
project_ideas.name: Framing-Paired Frontier Probe
project_ideas.poc: Construct paired task sets where each pair is one operation expressed two ways: a benchmark-framed version and an operational-automation-framed version embedded in a realistic workflow. Run many models across both framings.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Diogo Almeida
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: The state of AI, LLM alignment limitations, and the future of software engineering and agent design
  • Purpose: To challenge current industry assumptions about LLMs, RLHF, and agent design, and to advocate for software engineering practices that prioritize reliability and machine-native optimization over vibe coding. Diogo Almeida, co-founder of TypeSafe AI, presents a provocative critique of current AI trends. He argues that 100% of LLMs are optimized for assistance (RLHF) rather than automation, creating a cognitive dissonance where models are 'too good to be true' at reasoning benchmarks yet 'too bad to be useful' at real-world automation tasks. He compares the current LLM revolution to the discovery of the blue LED—an unexpected primitive that unlocked entirely new capabilities—and outlines a vision for machine-native AI, real software engineering (decomposition, encapsulation, state management), and reliable intelligence.

Topic Map

The Jagged Technological Frontier of AI

  • Explanation: AI capabilities are uneven: models excel at millenary math problems or creative generation yet fail completely at seemingly simple accounting or data entry tasks.
  • Key claims:
    • AI capabilities form a jagged frontier.
    • Models are superhuman at some tasks and useless at others.
  • Examples:
    • Passing complex benchmarks while failing simple accounting or drive-through automation.
  • Terminology:
    • Jagged frontier
    • Cognitive dissonance
  • Why it matters: Understanding the jagged frontier helps explain why general-purpose chatbots fall short in production automation.

The Two Cults in AI and RLHF Limitations

  • Explanation: Contrasting the hype cult of AGI believers who focus on benchmark scores with real-world users who see stagnation in core automation.
  • Key claims:
    • 100% of LLMs today are optimized for assistance via RLHF.
    • RLHF makes models too good to be true at assistance but bad at automation.
  • Examples:
    • ChatGPT vs. deep research and coding assistants.
  • Terminology:
    • RLHF
    • RLVR
    • Assistance vs. Automation
  • Why it matters: Highlighting why LLMs require a human-in-the-loop and how current alignment paradigms limit autonomous capabilities.

The Bitterer Lesson: Doing the Right Task

  • Explanation: Expanding on Sutton's bitter lesson, Almeida argues that data and doing the right task matter more than compute and algorithms alone.
  • Key claims:
    • Data always matters more than compute.
    • Doing the right task is the ultimate driver of performance breakthroughs.
  • Examples:
    • Pre-training next-token prediction versus RLHF alignment tasks.
  • Terminology:
    • Sutton's bitter lesson
    • Next-token prediction
  • Why it matters: Explains why task selection and data quality are more critical than raw model scale for practical applications.

Software Engineering for Machine-Native AI

  • Explanation: Advocating for real software engineering principles—decomposition, encapsulation, and state management—when building AI agents.
  • Key claims:
    • Software engineering needs to move beyond vibe coding.
    • Agents are constrained by the KV cache and lack shared state and memory management.
  • Examples:
    • Breaking tasks down into verifiable stages.
  • Terminology:
    • KV cache
    • State management
    • Encapsulation
    • Semantic dependent typing
  • Why it matters: Provides a blueprint for building robust, reliable AI agent architectures that scale.

Key Points

LLMs are optimized for assistance, not automation

  • Explanation: Current training pipelines like RLHF optimize models to be helpful assistants, which makes them unreliable for autonomous execution.
  • Evidence: Infamous failures of AI automation in simple workflows like drive-thrus.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must build systems that integrate code with AI decision-making rather than expecting end-to-end autonomy without verification.

Reliable intelligence vs. general intelligence

  • Explanation: The industry suffers from LLM Stockholm syndrome, focusing on broad capabilities instead of narrow, hyper-reliable intelligence.
  • Evidence: Getting 95% accuracy on general tasks is useless if reliability is needed 100% of the time.
  • Practical implication: Focus engineering efforts on narrow, highly verifiable agent workflows.

The analogy of the blue LED

  • Explanation: Just as the invention of the blue LED unlocked full-color displays and white lighting, machine-native primitives will unlock a software engineering revolution.
  • Evidence: Historical evolution of lighting technology.
  • Practical implication: New AI primitives will exponentially expand what software can achieve.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Machine-Native AI Framework

  • How it works: Rethinking software engineering by combining traditional software logic with AI decision-making primitives.
  • Components:
    • Decomposition
    • Encapsulation
    • State management
    • Semantic dependent typing
  • When to use: When building robust AI agent systems that require high reliability.

Examples & Case Studies

The introduction of RLHF in LLMs.

  • Illustrates: How alignment for assistance creates models that are great to chat with but poor at autonomous execution.
  • Lesson: You get what you optimize for.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Stop relying solely on benchmarks to evaluate production AI readiness.
    • Incorporate proper state management and task decomposition in agent design.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift focus from prompt engineering to reliable system architecture.
    • Embrace machine-native software engineering principles.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can memory be managed beyond the KV cache?
    • What would semantic dependent typing look like in production codebases?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • 100% of LLMs are optimized for assistance (RLHF) (factual claim)
  • Data always matters more than compute in achieving breakthrough performance (theoretical claim)

Notable Quotes

"What the fuck is actually going on and where is all the automation?" (at 0:37) "You get what you optimize for." (at 15:18)

Compressed Summary

  • LLMs are optimized for assistance through RLHF, limiting automation reliability.
  • Sutton's bitter lesson extended: data and doing the right task matter more than compute.
  • AI agent design is currently constrained by the KV cache and lack of shared state.
  • Real software engineering principles like decomposition and state management are essential for AI systems.
  • Keywords: llm, rlhf, agents, reliability, software-engineering
  • Core insight: Current LLMs are optimized for assistance rather than automation, necessitating a shift toward machine-native software engineering and rigorous state management for reliable AI systems.
